extracted.intended_audience: small businesses and applicants preparing SBIR/STTR proposals (federal small business grant proposers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for small-business proposers on how to prepare responsive SBIR/STTR proposals by understanding and addressing the evaluation criteria in solicitations. Covers what reviewers look for (innovation, team, commercialization, technical approach) and proposal-preparation practices (win themes, reviewer verification, independent review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ever-present evaluation criterion across SBIR/STTR solicitations; agencies frame it variously (e.g., DoD: “the soundness, technical merit and innovation of the proposed approach…”; HHS: asks whether the application “challenge[s] and seek[s] to shift current research or clinical practice paradigms by utilizing novel theoretical concepts, approaches or methodologies?”; DOE: evaluates innovativeness of idea and approach; NSF uses 'Intellectual Merit' instead of the word innovation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To demonstrate innovation you must show how your idea departs from current practice and why it is novel. Agencies may expect plans for developing and verifying the innovation (NASA) and evidence that the approach addresses a significant scientific/technical challenge. Tie claims of innovation to concrete comparisons with the state of the art (see separate criterion on literature/state of the art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the state of the art / literature review and contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposers must demonstrate an understanding of the current state of the art: review the literature and contrast your approach with conventional wisdom rather than assuming reviewers know the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly document the existing literature/technologies and use them as the baseline against which you show novelty. If you come from a non-academic background and this is unfamiliar, do the necessary review anyway — solicitations consistently require demonstration of knowledge of the state of the art and a clear call-out of what is innovative about your approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience, qualifications, and facilities (team capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: All agencies evaluate team qualifications and capacity to execute: e.g., DOE: “Ability to carry out the project in an efficient manner as evidenced by the qualifications of the Principal Investigator or PI, other key staff, subcontractors and consultants”; NSF: evaluates how well qualified the individual, team or organization is and if adequate resources are available; HHS and NASA have similar personnel/capability-focused criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that you CAN do the work — show personnel qualifications, institutional resources, past track record delivering comparable services. The government assesses risk; emphasize committed, available staff and facilities to minimize perceived risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization / commercial potential and feasibility / impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Many solicitations explicitly evaluate potential for commercialization and impact: HHS asks if the project has commercial potential and whether the Commercialization Plan demonstrates a high probability of commercialization; DoD looks at “potential for commercial applications”; DOE evaluates likelihood of leading to a marketable product and attracting further development funding; NASA evaluates 'Commercial Potential and Feasibility' including commercialization record and co-funding/Phase III commitments; NSF's 'broader impact' assesses societal benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear commercialization strategy/plan, evidence of market potential, and any commitments or prior commercialization experience. Address probability of market adoption, plans for Phase III follow-on funding, co-funding commitments, and how the work could attract further development investment after the SBIR/STTR project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific/Technical Approach / Strength and significance of approach (Significance / Intellectual Merit / Impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies assess the soundness and strength of the scientific/technical approach and the significance of the problem or challenge (e.g., DoD: soundness and technical merit; DOE: Strength of the Scientific/Technical Approach; NSF: Intellectual Merit; HHS: Significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe a rigorous, feasible approach that addresses a meaningful technical or scientific challenge. Explain methods, feasibility, and why the approach is likely to succeed; tie approach to the significance and potential to advance knowledge or solve an important problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to solicitation evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must be responsive to the specific evaluation criteria stated in each Funding Opportunity Announcement or solicitation; those criteria are usually listed toward the end of the solicitation document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before writing, locate and carefully read the solicitation’s evaluation-criteria section and use it as the blueprint for what to address in the proposal. Address each required criterion thoroughly and explicitly so reviewers can assess responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess win themes and competitive positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful proposers assess 'win themes' — how they stack up against evaluation criteria — to surface gaps and help decide which topics to pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the evaluation criteria to perform an early competitive assessment: identify strengths to emphasize (win themes), identify gaps (e.g., weak team or missing resources) and decide which solicitation topics to respond to. Convene colleagues or management soon after solicitation release to down-select and prioritize topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it easy for reviewers to verify responsiveness (call out criteria, emphasize strengths, mitigate weaknesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposers should include language within the proposal that clearly and subtly calls out evaluation criteria and emphasizes strengths relative to them; they may also disclose perceived weaknesses and explain mitigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure wording so reviewers can quickly find and confirm how you meet each criterion (explicit cross-references, summary statements). Where you anticipate reviewer concerns, acknowledge them and describe risk-mitigation steps rather than leaving issues implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent review and allow sufficient time for revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submission have another party independently review the draft and evaluate how the proposal stacks up against the evaluation criteria; allow sufficient time to address feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule independent/red-team reviews and build time in the timeline to incorporate reviewer feedback and fix gaps. Do not wait until the last minute — successful proposers allocate time for external review and revision to improve responsiveness to evaluation criteria.
